project.title: How QR Codes Store So Much Information
project.topic: How QR codes encode data in a grid of dark and light squares and use error correction
project.script: A QR code is more than a random pattern of squares. Its grid represents data using black and white modules, with special markers that help your camera detect the code's position and orientation. The pattern can encode text, website links, and other information. QR codes also include error correction, so a code may still scan even if part of it is dirty or damaged. Your phone reads the pattern, decodes the data, and then opens the link or displays the stored information.

project.title: How Noise-Cancelling Headphones Silence Noise
project.topic: How active noise cancellation uses microphones and opposing sound waves to reduce steady background noise
project.script: Noise-cancelling headphones don't simply block sound with thick padding. Tiny microphones listen to surrounding noise, and the headphones create another sound wave designed to oppose it. When the waves meet, they can partially cancel each other out. This works especially well for steady low sounds, like an airplane engine or air conditioner. Sudden voices and sharp noises are harder to remove because they change quickly. The headphones combine this active system with physical ear cups to make your surroundings quieter.

project.title: Why the Ocean Looks Blue
project.topic: How water absorbs longer wavelengths of visible light more strongly and scatters blue light
project.script: The ocean isn't blue just because it reflects the sky. Water absorbs red and orange wavelengths more strongly, while some blue light travels farther and scatters back toward your eyes. That gives deep, clear water its blue appearance. The exact color changes with depth, particles, algae, and the angle of the sunlight. Shallow water can look turquoise because light reflects off sand and the seabed. So the ocean's color comes from how light interacts with water and everything suspended or sitting beneath it.

project.title: Why Time Runs Differently Near a Black Hole
project.topic: How gravity affects the passage of time according to general relativity
project.script: Near a black hole, time can pass more slowly compared with time far away. Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that gravity affects the passage of time, and extremely strong gravity makes the difference dramatic. To someone watching from far away, a clock closer to the black hole appears to tick more slowly. But a person beside that clock would experience their own time normally. The effect depends on the observer and the gravitational environment; it's not that the nearby person feels time stop.

project.title: Why Some Airplanes Dump Fuel Before Landing
project.topic: Why certain large aircraft may jettison fuel in an emergency to reach a safe landing weight
project.script: Why would an airplane ever release fuel into the air? Some large aircraft can weigh too much to land immediately after takeoff, especially if an emergency forces them to return. Their maximum takeoff weight can be higher than their recommended landing weight. When conditions require it, a crew may jettison fuel to reduce weight before landing. Not every aircraft can do this, and crews may instead land overweight when that is safer. Fuel dumping is an unusual safety procedure, not a normal part of every flight.
